KEY MESSAGE 1: A deep (997 millibar) and large low pressure system currently in Virginia will be pulled north-northwestward into western Pennsylvania tonight and slightly strengthen. Satellite imagery shows a conveyor belt of rich moisture over the western Atlantic Ocean being drawn into the northeastern flank of this system, which will transport moderate to briefly heavy rainfall rates into our region. There has been a trend towards a larger footprint of ice accumulations within the Winter Weather Advisory area, especially in Vermont, as rain falls tonight. One reason is colder than expected air temperatures today resulting in road temperatures only reaching the middle 30s in much of the area. Mid-afternoon temperatures are only in the 30 to 33 range in much of central Vermont, and with every degree meaningful for the important freezing point as rain reaches the surface, the implications for ice accumulation are massive. As of now, we expect wet-bulb cooling at precipitation onset being offset by the very strong warm air advection associated with the plume of moisture. That being said, the rainfall amounts are fairly robust with high probalities of rainfall rates in excess of 0.06" concurrent with freezing rain, which is a proxy for signficant icing potential. Colder, drier northeasterly flow in the northern St. Lawrence Valley could lead to relatively efficient accretion and the majority of rain falling in the form of freezing rain. With ice-to-liquid ratios closer to 1, there is a high end potential for higher ice amounts than forecast which would lead to significant ice, in which power outages would occur due to its weight on trees and power lines. Meanwhile, the impacts in central Vermont near and east of the Green Mountains look relatively small with threat of heavier amounts limited to higher terrain with lower population, but travel may be difficult with even light ice amounts. Eventually, sometime Friday morning, temperatures will warm above freezing with all precipitation changing to rain. KEY MESSAGE 2: The swath of rain will be accompanied by strong easterly winds, which mostly will stay above the ground due to very stable air. However, we remain concerned for locally damaging winds, and confidence in occurence in eastern Rutland County led to an upgrade to a High Wind Warning. WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) -Happy Thanksgiving! The bulk of the Thanksgiving holiday is looking quiet and dry. We will notice more cloud cover through the day, but we look to stay dry through at least Thanksgiving evening and night. Rain showers and some high terrain mountain snow showers arrive to the south on Thanksgiving evening and push northward through the night. Overnight lows are in the mid to upper 30s for most. There could be some icing at the very onset of this system to start, with a few communities in higher terrain spots maybe running a glaze of icing. I am not expecting any big issues on the main roads, but a few secondary roads could become a tad slick tonight, especially in higher terrain spots. Black Friday will see any mountain mixed precipitation transition into mainly rain, and rain could be heavier at times, especially through the morning hours and becoming a bit more scattered by Friday evening and night. The other big component to this system looks to be the wind. That is why we have gone ahead and issued a First Alert Weather Day for Friday. The real bullseye for the wind will be right along the western slopes of the mountains, where they could see gusts upwards of 40-60 MPH. This could be enough to result in scattered power outages Friday. Intensity will vary widely over short distances. Ridgelines and communities on or near the western mountain slopes again could see a window of gusts as high as 40 to 60 mph early Friday. Conditions have to come together in the right way to see the higher end gusts make it to the ground. We usually see wind gusts intensify when rain slows down or stops. Gusts will be much less intense away from the western slopes. Some areas won’t see much wind at all. The strongest gusts will likely occur early Friday morning before sunrise, especially if there is a lull in precipitation. Wind will trend lighter through the morning and into Friday afternoon. Saturday looks drier overall, but there could still be a few scattered showers and mountain snow showers from time to time. Temperatures are again in the low to mid 40s. Winds look to be calmer through the day Saturday. By Sunday, most of us are back to dry conditions, but cloudy as temperatures continue to warm by a few degrees and we head back towards the mid and upper 40s and lower 50s. Into next week a few showers are possible by Monday with temperatures again in the mid to upper 40s.
